Our project, Abandoned But Not Forgotten, is an educational multimedia presentation created by Ophelia on Mars that chronicles the history, technology, and enduring legacy of robotic Mars exploration.

We developed a structured visual guide tracing Mars missions from early flybys and orbiters (Mariner 4, Mariner 9) and Viking landers to modern rovers (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, and Zhurong). Our presentation breaks down how robotic equipment functions, profiles major scientific discoveries, and highlights both the NASA engineering teams and the students who named the rovers.

This project addresses the challenge by examining what happens to spacecraft left behind on Mars once extreme cold, dust, or power loss ends their active service, demonstrating how their collected data remains valuable long after contact ends. It is important because these retired machines—having uncovered evidence of ancient water, organic molecules, and oxygen generation—continue to advance planetary science, inspire future innovators, and lay the essential groundwork for safe human exploration of Mars.
details:
What Our Project Does & How It Works

Abandoned But Not Forgotten (created by Ophelia on Mars) is an educational multimedia presentation that chronicles the history, engineering, discoveries, and enduring legacy of robotic Mars exploration.

Designed as a structured, infographic-style visual narrative, the project guides viewers through Mars exploration in progressive chapters:

  • Mission Purpose & Goals: Introduces why humanity sends spacecraft to Mars and breaks down the five core mission objectives—understanding the planet's history, studying past water, searching for signs of microbial life, analyzing geology and climate, and preparing for future human missions.
  • Chronological Timeline (1965–2021): Traces over five decades of exploration from early flybys and orbiters (Mariner 4 and Mariner 9) and stationary landers (Viking 1 & 2) to mobile surface rovers (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance).
  • Spacecraft Systems & Discoveries: Explains the four main types of exploration equipment (rovers, landers, orbiters, and scientific instruments), how rover subsystems operate, and six landmark scientific findings—including ancient riverbeds, iron-rich hematite "blueberries," organic molecules, and subsurface radar mapping by the Zhurong rover.
  • In-Depth NASA Rover Profiles: Compares the specs, power systems, instruments, and milestones of NASA's rovers, highlighting how missions like Sojourner (83 days vs. a 7-day plan) and Spirit & Opportunity (up to 15 years vs. a 90-sol design) far exceeded expectations, alongside Curiosity's discoveries in Gale Crater and Perseverance's work with the Ingenuity helicopter and MOXIE oxygen-generation experiment.
  • End-of-Mission Realities & Human Legacy: Examines the environmental and technical factors that retire rovers—dust accumulation, worn batteries, extreme cold, and communication loss—before spotlighting the NASA engineering teams and student essay-contest winners who brought these missions to life.

Benefits of the Project

  • Accessible STEM Education: Translates dense aerospace engineering data, mission timelines, and planetary science findings into visually scannable infographic modules suitable for students, educators, and general audiences.
  • Comprehensive Comparative Reference: Side-by-side mission cards make it easy to compare how rover technologies evolved from the 10.5 kg solar-powered Sojourner to the 1,025 kg plutonium-powered Perseverance.
  • Preserves Historical & Human Context: Connects technical milestones with the real scientists, engineers, and young students behind the missions, preventing retired spacecraft from being viewed merely as obsolete hardware.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to shift how audiences view spacecraft left behind on other worlds. Even when dust storms, freezing temperatures, or power depletion end a rover's active mission, these machines are physically left on Mars but never forgotten. By illustrating how their data continues to advance planetary science and lay the groundwork for safe human exploration, our project aims to spark curiosity in space science and inspire the next generation of young explorers, engineers, and dreamers.

Tools, Software & Resources Used

  • Graphic Design & Illustration Software: Used to create custom character illustrations, space-themed backgrounds, mission badges, and structured infographic layouts.
  • Presentation & Video Editing Software: Used to sequence the visual slides, apply smooth transitions, and synchronize the presentation with a cinematic instrumental soundtrack.
  • Scientific & Historical References: Built using publicly available NASA mission archives, rover technical specifications, mission photography, and historical records of NASA's student rover-naming contests. (Note: No custom coding languages or specialized hardware were required, as the project was developed as a digital multimedia presentation.)

How Our Project Is Creative

  • Original Mascot Storytelling: We combined custom anime-style astronaut character art ("Ophelia") with authentic NASA spacecraft photography and schematics, creating a welcoming visual guide that bridges playful illustration with real-world aerospace science.
  • Poster-Style Infographic Design: Rather than relying on plain text slides, every section is designed as a cohesive, high-contrast infographic card featuring bold typography, color-coded data callouts, and "Did You Know?" highlights.
  • Human-Centered Narrative Arc: Instead of ending with hardware specs, the presentation builds toward an emotional tribute—pairing the technical reality of why rovers stop working with the stories of the NASA teams who built them and the four students (ages 9 to 13) whose winning essays gave them their names.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific Accuracy: We carefully verified mission launch and landing dates, rover dimensions and mass, power sources (solar panels vs. nuclear MMRTGs), distance traveled, and milestone figures (such as Ingenuity's 72 flights and MOXIE's 122 grams of oxygen).
  • Clarity & Visual Hierarchy: Because Mars exploration spans decades of complex engineering, we structured information into bite-sized points, clear icons, and consistent visual layouts so viewers can absorb key takeaways effortlessly.
  • Balance Between Technical Depth & Inspiration: We intentionally balanced technical specifications with big-picture storytelling so the project appeals both to space enthusiasts looking for mission facts and to younger viewers discovering Mars exploration for the first time.
